frames.narration: A client opens a TCP connection to the virtual address 203.0.113.10, port 443. Every balancer node announces this address over BGP, so the router has eight equal-cost paths to it. The router hashes the 5-tuple and picks the path to balancer node 7. All later packets of this connection hash the same way.

Node 7 has no entry for this flow. It hashes the 5-tuple to 20,114 and reads that slot of its Maglev table, a 65,537-slot array in which every slot names a healthy backend. The slot says b42, and the node records the choice in its flow table.

Node 7 forwards the packet to b42. In direct server return mode, only the destination changes. The backend replies straight to the client, with the virtual address as the source, so the large response never passes through a balancer.

In the background the health checkers probe b42 every 2 seconds, with a rule of 3 failures in a row to mark it down. They publish the results, and the balancers rebuild their tables when the list changes. All is healthy for now.
Balancer node 5 is replaced during a rollout. The router now has seven paths, rehashes the connections, and this client's next packet lands on node 3, which has never seen the flow.

Node 3 has the same backend list, so it builds the identical table. Slot 20,114 still says b42, and the packet goes there. The connection carries on without the client noticing, which a plain modulo hash could not do.

Later, b42 is taken out for a deployment. The control plane puts it in the draining state: it receives no new connections, but this one is left alone. When the connection ends or the 5-minute drain timeout passes, b42 is removed, and only the flows that were on it had to move.
